summary: Jonah is angry that Nineveh has been spared, and he explains that he fled because he knew Yahweh is gracious, merciful, slow to anger, and willing to relent from harm. Outside the city, a vine gives him shade until a worm makes it wither; a hot wind and the sun then intensify his discomfort, and he again says he would rather die. The book ends by comparing concern for the short-lived plant with concern for Nineveh, its people, and its animals.
whyItMatters: This final chapter gives Jonah’s delayed explanation for his flight and turns the whole book toward the question of divine concern for outsiders. It leaves readers with an unanswered question rather than Jonah’s reply.

context.author: The book narrates events about Jonah son of Amittai but does not identify its author.
context.audience: No audience is named; the story addresses readers familiar with Israel’s God and presses them to consider mercy, wrongdoing, and people beyond their own community.
context.date: The narrated prophet is linked with the eighth century BCE through 2 Kings, but the book’s composition date is disputed and no exact year is secure.
context.setting: The book moves from Jonah’s flight toward Tarshish to Nineveh, an Assyrian city; chapter 4 takes place in and just outside Nineveh, east of the city.
context.literaryForm: A prophetic story with short speeches, irony, repeated reversals, and a closing question.

outline.heading: Jonah objects to mercy
outline.note: Jonah is angry, explains that he fled because he knew Yahweh’s merciful character, asks to die, and receives Yahweh’s first question about his anger.

outline.heading: Jonah waits outside the city
outline.note: Jonah leaves the city, builds a booth east of it, and waits to see what will happen.

outline.heading: The vine brings relief
outline.note: Yahweh God prepares a vine to shade Jonah, and Jonah becomes exceedingly glad because of it.

outline.heading: Shade lost; heat intensifies
outline.note: God prepares a worm and a sultry east wind; the vine withers, the sun beats on Jonah, and he again says it is better to die than live.

outline.heading: The final question
outline.note: God questions Jonah’s anger over the vine, then contrasts Jonah’s concern for the short-lived vine with divine concern for Nineveh, its more than one hundred twenty thousand persons, and many animals.

keyVerses.text: He prayed to Yahweh, and said, “Please, Yahweh, wasn’t this what I said when I was still in my own country? Therefore I hurried to flee to Tarshish, for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and you relent of doing harm.
keyVerses.why: This is Jonah’s own explanation for his flight and anger: he expected mercy, and he resented it when it reached Nineveh.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh said, “Is it right for you to be angry?”
keyVerses.why: Yahweh’s question frames the chapter as an examination of Jonah’s anger, not simply a report of it.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh God prepared a vine and made it to come up over Jonah, that it might be a shade over his head to deliver him from his discomfort. So Jonah was exceedingly glad because of the vine.
keyVerses.why: The vine gives Jonah personal relief and becomes the object lesson for the final comparison.

keyVerses.text: Shouldn’t I be concerned for Nineveh, that great city, in which are more than one hundred twenty thousand persons who can’t discern between their right hand and their left hand, and also many animals?”
keyVerses.why: The book closes with this unanswered question, setting Jonah’s concern for the vine beside God’s concern for the city and its animals.

questions.question: Why is Jonah angry at the beginning of the chapter?
questions.answer: The chapter says Jonah is displeased and angry after the city has been spared. In his prayer, he explains that he fled because he knew Yahweh to be gracious, merciful, slow to anger, abundant in loving kindness, and willing to relent from harm. His anger is aimed at the mercy he expected God to show.

questions.question: What does Jonah’s prayer reveal about why he fled to Tarshish?
questions.answer: Jonah says that while he was still in his own country he expected this outcome, and therefore hurried to flee to Tarshish. The chapter gives this as his stated motive: he knew God’s merciful character and did not want that mercy extended to Nineveh.

questions.question: What does “relent of doing harm” mean here?
questions.answer: In Jonah’s words, Yahweh can turn from carrying out threatened harm. The chapter does not present this as God confessing wrongdoing; it describes a changed course of action toward the city. This fits the book’s larger movement from announced judgment to spared Nineveh.

questions.question: Why does Jonah ask to die twice?
questions.answer: Jonah first asks Yahweh to take his life after explaining his anger over mercy for Nineveh. Later, after the vine withers and the sun and wind strike him, he again says it is better to die than live. The chapter presents these words as Jonah’s distress and anger, not as instruction for readers or as a diagnosis.

questions.question: What is the point of the booth and the vine?
questions.answer: Jonah builds a booth east of the city and waits to see what will happen. God then provides a plant whose shade delights him. WEB calls it a vine, KJV and Brenton a gourd, and Douay-Rheims ivy; the Hebrew qiqayon has prompted different botanical identifications. Its role in the argument is clear even without a settled species: Jonah values its shade, then resents losing it.

questions.question: Why are the worm and the east wind included?
questions.answer: The chapter says God prepared both the worm and the sultry east wind, just as Yahweh God prepared the vine. The worm removes Jonah’s shade, and the wind and sun expose his discomfort. These events lead to the second question about whether Jonah’s anger is right.

questions.question: Is Jonah right to be angry?
questions.answer: The chapter does not endorse Jonah’s answer. Yahweh asks him twice whether his anger is right, first in general and then about the vine. Jonah insists he is right to be angry “even to death,” but the final divine question challenges that judgment rather than confirming it.

questions.question: Who are the “more than one hundred twenty thousand persons” in the last verse?
questions.answer: The text describes them as persons who cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand. Readers differ on whether this phrase refers specifically to children or more broadly to people lacking discernment. The chapter itself does not turn the number into a full population estimate; it uses the number to press the question of concern for Nineveh.

questions.question: Why does the final verse mention animals?
questions.answer: The animals are included in Yahweh’s closing question, not left as background. The comparison moves from Jonah’s concern for a vine he did not grow to God’s concern for a great city with many people and many animals. The book ends there, without giving Jonah a final reply.

glossary.def: The destination Jonah says he fled toward; its precise identification is disputed, but in this chapter it marks his attempted escape from the mission involving Nineveh.
A phrase Jonah uses for God’s merciful character when explaining why he expected Yahweh to spare Nineveh.
A temporary shelter Jonah makes east of the city so he can sit in the shade and watch what will happen.
The plant Yahweh God prepares to shade Jonah; Jonah is glad about it, then angry when it withers.
The creature God prepares at dawn to chew the vine so that it withers.
The great city at the center of the chapter’s final question, containing more than one hundred twenty thousand persons and many animals.
